Professor Jens Blauert is an eminent figure in German acoustics, known for his pioneering research in psychoacoustics and spatial hearing.

An article I posted earlier was in fact based on one of Professor Blauert’s papers: Two ears “reading” the world

Background and career

Jens Blauert was born on June 20, 1938, in Hamburg, Germany. He went to primary and secondary school in Dresden and Hamburg, then studied communications engineering at RWTH Aachen University, where he received his doctorate in engineering in 1969. In 1973 he completed his habilitation at TU Berlin, and in 1974 he was appointed full professor at Ruhr University Bochum. There he founded the Institute of Communication Acoustics (IKA), which he directed for 29 years until his retirement in 2003. He was then made professor emeritus and has held visiting professorships at universities around the world, including a distinguished visiting professorship in the architectural acoustics program at Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute in the United States.

Blauert is a fellow of several learned societies, including the Acoustical Society of America (ASA), the Institute of Electrical and Electronics Engineers (IEEE), the Institute of Acoustics (UK) and the Audio Engineering Society (AES). He is also an honorary member of the German Society of Audiology and the Polish Acoustical Society. In 1999 the ASA awarded him its Helmholtz-Rayleigh Interdisciplinary Silver Medal for his contributions to sound localization, concert hall acoustics, signal processing and acoustical standards.

Main research areas

Blauert’s research spans many subfields of acoustics, including spatial hearing, binaural technology, aural architecture, perceptual quality, speech technology, virtual environments and telepresence. His work focuses in particular on how humans perceive and localize sound, which has had a profound influence on audio technology and architectural design.

Sound localization

Sound localization is at the heart of Blauert’s research. He investigated how humans determine the direction of a sound from the interaural time difference (ITD) and interaural level difference (ILD). His research showed that certain frequency ranges are especially important for these localization cues. For example, low frequencies (100 Hz to 1,000 Hz) lend themselves to detecting ITDs, while high frequencies (above 1,000 Hz) are better suited to ILDs, which is related to the head-shadow effect. His doctoral thesis, a study of sound localization in the median plane with the head immobilized (1969, Acustica), laid the groundwork for this field.

His book Spatial Hearing: The Psychophysics of Human Sound Localization (1983) became the standard reference in the field, with a detailed treatment of the psychophysical mechanisms of sound localization. It is widely cited, particularly in the development of audio systems and hearing aids, and it highlights the role of specific frequency bands.

Binaural technology

Blauert’s contributions to binaural technology are just as significant. Binaural technology uses two microphones to mimic the way our two ears hear, creating a three-dimensional listening experience. His research improved the accuracy of binaural recording and reproduction, making sound more immersive in music, games and virtual reality. In virtual reality, for example, a sound can arrive from a specific direction around the listener, heightening the sense of being there. His work has been applied in audio engineering and the entertainment industry, especially in the development of 3D audio and immersive experiences.

Architectural acoustics

Blauert’s research also extended to architectural acoustics, the design of spaces with the best possible acoustic properties. His work influenced the design of concert halls, theaters and other performance spaces, helping ensure that sound is evenly distributed and clearly perceived. His institute, the IKA, for example, focused on communication acoustics and studied how architectural design can optimize sound reflections and perceived quality. His research gave architects guidance on how to give audiences the best possible listening experience from every seat.

Impact and applications

Blauert’s work has had a far-reaching impact in several fields:

  • Audio technology

    : His research on sound localization helped bring about more realistic audio systems and hearing aids, improving the quality of life of people with hearing loss.

  • Virtual reality

    : Advances in binaural technology have deepened immersion in virtual reality, making games and simulation training more lifelike.

  • Architectural design

    : Research on aural architecture has improved the acoustic performance of concert halls and theaters, and with it the audience’s enjoyment.

Publications and honors

Blauert has published prolifically: more than 150 papers and several books, including Spatial Hearing: The Psychophysics of Human Sound Localization (1983) and Acoustics for Engineers: Troy Lectures (2009), co-authored with Ning Xiang. His work has been cited more than 7,837 times, a measure of its broad reach in academia.

His many honors include an honorary doctorate (Dr. techn.) from Aalborg University in Denmark in 1994 and the ASA Silver Medal in 1999. Over his career he also served as president of the German Acoustical Society (DEGA) and as an advisor to several international scientific organizations.

Open questions and debates

Although Blauert’s research is widely recognized, some technical details, such as the precise boundaries of particular frequency bands, can vary with research methods and applications. Different studies may disagree about the optimal frequency ranges, for instance, but on the whole his contributions are regarded as foundational to the field.

The table below summarizes Blauert’s main contributions and their impact:

Conclusion

Professor Jens Blauert’s career shows how acoustics research shapes technology and everyday life. His work has not only advanced theoretical understanding but has also found practical use in audio technology, virtual reality and architectural design. His legacy will continue to inspire future scientists and engineers to explore the mysteries of sound.
